style_when: the article is a purely conceptual synthesis or policy dilemma where no physical facility, machine, or supply chain exists, and an elegant abstract paper silhouette states the idea. Never reach for paper collage when the story describes physical manufacturing, freight, energy, hardware, or heavy infrastructure — use cinematic still or telephoto industry instead
prompt: A minimalist editorial cut-paper collage on a control room console desk. Left of centre stands a tall cut-paper bucket made of dark slate-grey paper with a visible circular hole near its base; from the hole a thin stream of tiny cut-paper dots flows right, pooling into a clean rectangular stack of blank ivory pages representing a hundred-item page. A single oversized blank page lies under the bucket as a scale plate. Raking warm light from the left casts long physical paper shadows; palette graphite, bone white, safety yellow accent on the bucket rim; hand-torn rag paper with visible fibre, no legible print, generous negative space, off-centre asymmetric composition.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, legible numbers, UI, logos
rationale: This is a purely conceptual API rate-limit story with no physical facility, so a cut-paper collage can state the bucket-and-page mechanism symbolically without falling into datacenter stock; the bucket with a hole is the article's own framing, and the blank pages represent the only free lever.
subject: a leaking cut-paper request bucket beside a blank hundred-item page stack
core_thesis: A vendor's rate limit is a budget counted in requests, so the page size decides whether a nightly sync finishes long before the plan ladder does.
core_conflict: The paid plan ladder only multiplies the budget by three, while the free page-size lever multiplies it by one hundred, so the real bottleneck is hidden in the request shape.
